primary_claim: In a synthetic CodeNames sandwiching environment, scalable oversight protocols (consultancy, critiques) fully compensate for the simulated overseer flaws they target and reach performance similar to a robust-overseer baseline, requiring a stronger adversarial incentive to elicit reward hacking than the base protocol, though at greater compute cost; neither protocol covers for overseer bias.

effect.metric: reduction in true score vs overseer score under adversarial incentive
effect.value: base protocol: adversarial strength 0.375 causes ~0.65 reduction in true score but only ~0.05 reduction in overseer score; critiques protocol requires adversarial strength 0.75 for a smaller ~0.3 reduction in true score with ~0.05 reduction in overseer score

stated_future_work: identifying how humans are biased in their final judgments seems like an important area of future study, since neither protocol covers for overseer bias
expect the critiques protocol to be relatively more efficient for larger games than tested here
limitations_stated: neither the consultancy nor critiques protocol covers for overseer bias
results come from a single simplified CodeNames environment rather than a real deployment-relevant task
unsure of the underlying cause of the oracle being more sensitive to adversarial incentive than the LLM
effects were strongest in the base protocol; a larger effect might appear in other protocols with longer training runs
training runs still don't seem to have fully converged despite ~2 orders of magnitude more data than initial attempts
quote: scalable oversight techniques can fully compensate for different overseer flaws and still train the model to a similar level of performance as a non-scalable technique with a robust overseer
